question: A data service doubles its worker nodes but a global lock serializes every transaction. What is the most defensible performance prediction?
options: The lock can remain the bottleneck; adding nodes alone does not guarantee useful speed-up
CAP theorem guarantees perfect scalability
Replication automatically removes any global coordination
Throughput must double because the cluster has twice the CPUs
explanation: A serial critical section limits speed-up and may dominate throughput. Horizontal scaling only helps when meaningful work can be partitioned and coordination costs remain manageable.
source: L9 Scalable Data Management slides 2-4 (scale-out, throughput and cloud elasticity).

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes sharding from replication?
options: Sharding is only possible in a shared-memory machine
Replication increases the amount of distinct logical data stored without any extra disk usage
Sharding distributes distinct records; replication maintains redundant copies of the same records
Sharding and replication both mean duplicating every record onto every node
explanation: Sharding partitions responsibility for records, while replication creates redundant copies for availability, locality or reads. They can be combined but have different capacity and consistency effects.
source: L9 slides 3-6 (shared-nothing/cloud distribution and storage); Özsu & Valduriez, Principles of Distributed Database Systems, ch. 10, pp. 449-456.

question: Two replicas are disconnected. DB1 accepts write x = 10; DB2 has x = 0. To preserve linearizable reads during the partition, what must DB2 avoid?
options: Losing availability for that request
Refusing a request it cannot answer consistently
Blocking until it can determine a safe result
Returning the stale x = 0 as if it were current after the completed write
explanation: Serving x=0 after a completed x=10 write would violate the single-copy latest-value view if the write is ordered before the read. A CP-style choice can block or reject the read at DB2, sacrificing availability.
source: L9 slides 7-10 (CAP and replication); Özsu & Valduriez, ch. 11 §11.1 (CAP meaning).

question: A web application reads shopping carts almost exclusively by cart ID and wants flexible values at large scale. Which data model is the most natural primary fit?
options: A pure OLAP cube indexed exclusively by date
A static PDF archive with no query API
Key-value store
Graph-only traversal store
explanation: The key-value model directly supports access by known key and a flexible value. It does not by itself provide rich joins or arbitrary relationship traversals.
source: L9 slides 11-13 and 19 (NoSQL families and key-value stores); Özsu & Valduriez, ch. 11 §11.2.

question: An investigation repeatedly traverses relationships among suspects, companies, addresses and transactions. Which database model best matches the central query pattern?
options: Key-value store without any secondary structure
Graph data model with explicit edges and traversal operations
A data lake that does not permit graph processing
Document storage alone because relationships never matter
explanation: Graph stores represent entities and links directly, making multi-hop traversals and pattern queries a natural operation. Simple key-value lookup has no inherent graph traversal language.
source: L9 slides 16 and 19 (graph DBMS and workload mapping); Özsu & Valduriez, ch. 11 §11.5.

question: Why might an enterprise prefer a NewSQL/distributed SQL system over a simple key-value store for a transactional ledger?
options: It offers relational SQL and transactional semantics while aiming to distribute workload; coordination still costs something
It guarantees zero network latency for cross-partition transactions
It prevents use of secondary indexes and joins
It necessarily sacrifices all transaction guarantees to scale
explanation: NewSQL aims to combine SQL/ACID-style transactional capabilities with distributed scaling. It does not eliminate costs of consensus, coordination and multi-partition operations.
source: L9 slides 18-19 (NewSQL goals and use cases); Özsu & Valduriez, ch. 11 §11.6.

question: What is the defining challenge a polystore addresses?
options: Removing the need to translate queries or reconcile schema semantics
Replacing every data model with a single flat text file
Making multiple heterogeneous stores queryable through a coordinated interface and processing plan
Forcing every source to use one identical physical storage engine
explanation: Polystores integrate SQL, NoSQL and other engines while retaining specialized stores. Query translation, placement of computation and heterogeneous semantics are central difficulties.
source: L9 slides 20-24 (polystores, loose/tight coupling); Özsu & Valduriez, ch. 11 §11.7.

question: Which feature is characteristic of the original Google File System (GFS) design described in the assigned distributed storage reading?
options: A central master manages metadata and clients transfer all file payload through it
Files are stored in chunks at chunk servers, and clients obtain locations from the master then access chunk servers
Each client must copy every file in its entirety before any read
It stores only relational rows in a conventional OLTP table
explanation: GFS separates metadata management (master) from chunk payload storage (chunk servers). After locating chunks via the master, clients read data from chunk servers rather than routing file bytes through the master.
source: Özsu & Valduriez, Principles of Distributed Database Systems, ch. 10, printed pp. 453-456 (GFS architecture).

question: A distributed table is hash-partitioned by customer_id, but one customer produces most traffic. Why can adding workers fail to improve this workload?
options: Skew is possible only in a single-machine DBMS
Increasing workers always reduces per-key coordination
Hash partitioning always redistributes one hot key across all workers
The hotspot may remain assigned to one partition/worker, making it the straggler
explanation: All records for one join/partition key may map to the same worker. That worker dominates latency, so extra idle workers provide little benefit unless the design addresses hot keys or skew.
source: L9 slides 2-4 (partitionable scale-out) and Özsu & Valduriez ch. 11 (distributed partitioning); applied reasoning.
